doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Touring, Ella Fitzgerald and South America
title: Mack the Knife in Berlin
summary: How the Berlin concert was recorded and whether anyone sensed its significance.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: And that tour with Ella included the concert in Germany and Mack the Knife.

Oh, yeah. Mack the Knife, right. Yeah, I kept it. I said, “Ella, don’t do that. Do…” (laughs) Yeah. Well, that’s funny, too, because I didn’t… when Ella died, this guy who has a radio show, whose name I forget. He sort of has to know all the answers. But I told him about the recording and he was arguing with me over the phone. We had this… Pete Cavallo was our road manager. A great guy. And Norman Granz said… anyway, Pete schlepped all this recording equipment around on the trains and everything. And we went into the place in Berlin, and he just set the stuff up and turned it on. But the word got around that Norman Granz had been there and done all this stuff, and I was, I said, “Schmuck, I was there, you know. I might have been drunk, but I was actually there.” (laughs) Which, he just plugged it in and she sang great. And… (laughs) Yeah, she was incredible. But I think she messed up one thing on the Academy Awards, ‘cause it was a quick change of key, and she, she had never heard the arrangement before.
The Mack the Knife concert, did anybody that night in the group have a sense that that was going to be a major historical event that was going to live on forever?

No. (laughs) I don’t think so. We just had a lotta fun. And… I won’t say it was just another night. But it was an honor working with her, you know. And she sounded like she was having a ball, as well, on the record so…
